title.vi: Nhịp điệu chống lại bản quyền

hook.en: Dancehall’s interactive, collaborative nature doesn’t treat a work as isolated or even something that is “finished.” Iteration is a part of the creative process that is decided by the next function or party. In Larisa Kingston Mann’s “Rude Citizenship,” she outlines how copyright law was written at a time when many of the island’s people were themselves considered property under slavery, thereby creating — from the very start — a contentious relationship with those holding the society’s wealth. Copyright law was set up for those with ample resources to dictate what could be protected and who could profit.
hook.vi: Bản chất mang tính tương tác và cộng tác của dòng nhạc dancehall không coi một tác phẩm là biệt lập hay thậm chí là thứ gì đó “hoàn thiện”. Sự lặp đi lặp lại và cải tiến là một phần của quá trình sáng tạo do sự kiện hoặc bên tiếp theo quyết định. Trong cuốn “Rude Citizenship” (Quyền công dân bất trị) của Larisa Kingston Mann, bà phác thảo cách luật bản quyền được soạn thảo vào thời điểm mà nhiều người dân trên hòn đảo bản thân họ bị coi là tài sản dưới chế độ nô lệ, qua đó tạo ra — ngay từ đầu — một mối quan hệ đầy tranh cãi với những kẻ nắm giữ sự giàu có của xã hội. Luật bản quyền được thiết lập cho những kẻ có nguồn lực dồi dào để quyết định điều gì có thể được bảo vệ và ai có thể thu lợi.

sections.body_en: Beat-sharing directly challenges [p:neo-colonial copyright]’s individualistic definition of ownership and originality. Traditional copyright promotes monopoly over expression, enforced by harsh legal mechanisms (such as statutory damages) that make intertextuality, reuse, and artistic experimentation legally risky. Even Sean Paul, one of the most commercially successful dancehall artists in the world, attributed his mainstream success of “Get Busy” to the Diwali Riddim. If not for this collective creativity and shared use, we would not see dancehall music evolve and get pushed to the world in the way that it has.

Collective sharing didn’t stop at just music; dance was often learned collectively as well. I used to watch “passa passa” videos in high school and college, just to learn and keep up to date with the latest dances coming out of Jamaica and New York City in the early 2000s. These parties were the bane of anyone entrenched in respectability. The clothes were outlandish, the manners “rude,” the dancehall queens nothing short of acrobatic, and the parties could go until 6:00 a.m.

But this was also the time when new artists could get a slot, vendors could make a little money, and producers could collaborate with artists and get public consensus on what worked before dropping money at a studio.

The Caribbean has long been exploited on the world stage in many ways, and copyright law is no exception.

Jamaica was often sidelined into less than favourable international trade agreements that didn’t keep the interests of the Jamaican masses in mind. More often than not, there was a strict one-size-fits-all structure, dictated by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank: detrimental loan structures, one-sided economic trade agreements, currency devaluation, and exploitative labour guidelines.

In 1992, the IMF created terms that heavily impacted Jamaica’s economy. This served as the backdrop for the [y:Jamaica Copyright Act of 1993], when the country was directed to reshape its laws to participate in global trade. More rigid terms forced artists to start registering “riddims,” and while these laws are purported to protect artists, less resourced and independent artists struggled to make claims against large producers. This also killed the “handshake agreements” many artists and producers made prior to 1993.

A dancehall party flyer. Photo courtesy of OpenVerse. Public Domain.

This hasn’t stopped dancehall creators from organising alternative circuits of commerce and performance, social intimacy, and communal engagement. Even today, the continuous nature of dancehall works still causes friction with how copyright laws function.

This year, a monumental copyright case was overturned by a U.S. federal judge who named many famous artists in a list of [y:150], and affected about [y:2,000 tracks]. The plaintiffs, Cleveland “Clevie” Browne and the heirs of Wycliffe “Steely” Johnson**,** claimed that the “Fish Market” riddim (also known as the “Pocoman Jam riddim”) was the basis and source of the percussion pattern that runs through reggaeton, the now billion-dollar musical genre with origins in the Spanish reggae of Panama brought by Afro-Jamaican migrants, and further magnified by Puerto Rican artists.

However, the logic was denied. As US District Judge André Birotte Jr. said, “Plaintiffs have not clearly identified what copyrighted work contains the allegedly protectable selection and arrangement they seek to enforce.”

The claim failed to take all selections and arrangements mentioned and tie them to one work. But rather, it referenced a collection of works that mirrored parts over time: “That principle is especially significant here. Skidmore cautioned that a plaintiff cannot ‘reconstitut\[e\] the copyrighted work as a combination of unprotectable elements’ and then claim that those elements are substantially similar because they appear in an accused work, even where the elements are presented in ‘a different aesthetic context.’”

The nature of riddims is a double-edged sword here. Browne and Johnson were deprived of a chance to share in the profits of their creativity that set the groundwork for a whole new genre of music. If this lawsuit had gone in their favour, the logic could potentially have put any new reggaeton artist to this profit-sharing standard, possibly resulting in conditions only well-backed artists like Bad Bunny could afford to accommodate. Such an outcome could have created a disempowering dynamic for new artists. A power structure riddims fought in the first place.

We can all easily hear the main percussion in Puerto Rican reggaeton and Dominican dembow, but [p:copyright’s ears are selectively biased against rhythm] — usually favouring money, the artist’s will to attribute credit to where it’s due, and when the tracks were created in the more popular artist’s career. In fact, Black artists are often credited much later for genre-defining work and after lighter-skinned artists have made their money.

Despite the mainstream push away from collective processes, dancehall continues to evolve. What “makes Jamaicans cool” is the layers of understanding that come with what we share. Copyright creates a stamp in time — a piece of “the cool” the mainstream can manage to freeze and sell. Yet, the true cool develops alongside the collective and remains protected by that shared understanding.

keyPoint.en: Copyright law is like a rigid fence built across a flowing river, trying to freeze water that was meant to nourish a whole community. How can you support collaborative and shared creativity in your own daily work or artistic pursuits instead of locking ideas away?
keyPoint.vi: Luật bản quyền giống như một hàng rào cứng nhắc dựng lên giữa dòng sông đang chảy, cố gắng đóng băng nguồn nước vốn dùng để nuôi dưỡng cả một cộng đồng. Làm thế nào bạn có thể hỗ trợ sự sáng tạo mang tính cộng tác và chia sẻ trong công việc hàng ngày hoặc theo đuổi nghệ thuật của riêng mình thay vì khóa kín các ý tưởng?

en: Share a creative resource or idea with your peers without demanding exclusive ownership.
Support independent creators by engaging with their work directly rather than through corporate intermediaries.
Explore how collaborative cultures shape modern art forms by listening to diverse musical genres.
vi: Chia sẻ một tài nguyên sáng tạo hoặc ý tưởng với đồng nghiệp mà không đòi hỏi quyền sở hữu độc quyền.
Hỗ trợ các nhà sáng tạo độc lập bằng cách tương tác trực tiếp với tác phẩm của họ thay vì thông qua các bên trung gian doanh nghiệp.
Khám phá cách các nền văn hóa hợp tác định hình các loại hình nghệ thuật hiện đại bằng cách lắng nghe các thể loại âm nhạc đa dạng.
